security_spec.violation_condition: On a RISC-V hart where hardware implements Ssamb (interrupt code 14 masked as local), FreeBSD's intc_init_secondary() unconditionally sets SIE[14] via csr_set(sie, 1<<14) during AP boot (iterating irq=0..15 in intc.c:243). If the hardware subsequently asserts MIP[14], the trap flows through exception.S -> trap.c do_trap_supervisor/do_trap_user -> intc_intr() where active_irq=14 passes the >=INTC_NIRQS(16) guard, but intr_isrc_dispatch on the handlerless isrcs[14] fails. The stray-isr path in intc.c:284 calls intc_disable_intr() which does csr_clear(sie, 1<<14), yet NOTHING clears the SIP[14] pending bit. If any code path re-enables SIE[14] (e.g., intc re-init across suspend/resume, or a driver blindly re-enabling all sources), the latched pending bit causes immediate re-entry, forming a tight interrupt storm. For bhyve: hideleg only delegates bits 2/6/10 (vmm_riscv.c:155), so interrupt 14 traps to HS-mode during guest execution where no handler exists, potentially halting the host.
security_spec.summary: Ssamb repurposes reserved interrupt 14 as a local interrupt; FreeBSD's intc blindly enables all 16 IRQ slots on AP boot without Ssamb awareness, creating a stray-interrupt storm if hardware asserts MIP[14] before a handler is registered—and bhyve's hideleg omits it, risking HS-mode traps from guest execution

findings.finding: INTC_NIRQS is hardcoded to 16, causing the AP boot loop (irq=0..15) to unconditionally call intc_enable_intr() → csr_set(sie, 1<<irq) for interrupt sources 12-15, which are beyond the standard RISC-V local interrupt definitions (0=USIP .. 11=MEIP) and include reserved/local-extension interrupts. On hardware implementing Ssamb (LAMBI, interrupt code 14), this enables a handlerless isrc[14] at boot.

The guard `active_irq >= INTC_NIRQS` (line 278) passes for active_irq=14 (14 < 16). The stray-interrupt path at line 282-285 calls intc_disable_intr() → csr_clear(sie, 1<<14), which clears the SIE enable bit but does NOT clear the SIP[14] pending bit. If any code path subsequently re-enables SIE[14] (e.g., suspend/resume re-init, or a driver calling intc_enable_intr on all sources), the latched SIP[14] bit causes immediate re-trap, forming a tight interrupt storm with no exit condition.

intc_disable_intr() only clears the SIE enable bit via csr_clear(sie, 1ul<<irq) but never clears the corresponding SIP pending bit. Since the RISC-V spec requires SIP bits to be cleared by writing 1 to them (csr_set(sip, 1<<irq)), a stray interrupt's pending state survives the disable operation, enabling the interrupt-storm re-entry scenario.

intc_enable_intr() blindly performs csr_set(sie, 1ul<<irq) for any irq < INTC_NIRQS (0-15) without checking whether the interrupt source is architecturally valid or has a registered handler. Interrupt codes 12-15 correspond to reserved/local RISC-V extensions (COFI, LAMBI, etc.) that FreeBSD does not handle.

intc_attach registers isrc entries for all 16 interrupt sources (0-15). Interrupts 0 (IRQ_SOFTWARE_SUPERVISOR=1) is marked INTR_ISRCF_IPI; all others including undefined sources 12-15 are marked INTR_ISRCF_PPI. Since intr_isrc_init_on_cpu() only returns true when isrc_handlers>0, unregistered sources 12-15 are harmless until a handler is attached — but the isrc registration exists, allowing a hypothetical buggy driver to attach a handler to source 14.

hideleg only delegates bits 2 (VSSIP), 6 (VSTIP), and 10 (VSEIP) to VS-mode. All other local interrupts including 14 (LAMBI) trap to HS-mode during guest execution. The bhyve vmmops_run() loop (line 460-467 in riscv_handle_world_switch) catches interrupt-triggered HS-mode traps and exits with VM_EXITCODE_BOGUS. This causes the guest to be kicked out on any LAMBI assertion, but the host's stray-handler path (intc_intr) inherits the same SIP[14]-not-cleared bug as the non-bhyve path. In HS-mode, the interrupt remains enabled via sie[14] set during intc_init_secondary.

do_trap_supervisor correctly dispatches all interrupt-cause traps to the intr_irq_handler framework without filtering. The framework's root handler (intc_intr) is responsible for dispatch/rejection. This is architecturally correct — the filtering belongs at the PIC layer.
do_trap_user similarly dispatches all interrupt traps to the PIC framework. User-mode interrupt handling is architecturally correct.

The exception vectors save/restore the full trapframe (all GPRs, sepc, sstatus, stval, scause) and correctly transition between supervisor and user contexts. No CSR leakage across privilege boundaries.
findings.snippet:
save_registers 1
mv a0, sp
call _C_LABEL(do_trap_supervisor)
load_registers 1
sret

findings.finding: The thread context-switch path saves/restores callee-saved registers via PCB and invokes pmap_activate_sw for ASID/PMAP transition. FPE state (sstatus.FS) is correctly tracked, saved on dirty, and restored on activation. No interrupt-related CSR leakage across thread switches.
findings.snippet:
sd ra, (PCB_RA)(x13)
sd sp, (PCB_SP)(x13)
/* s[0-11] saved/restored */
call _C_LABEL(pmap_activate_sw)
